title: Review of acoustic comfort evaluation in dwellings—part I: Associations of acoustic field data to subjective responses from building surveys
research_question: To collect and examine studies combining acoustic field data and subjective responses in dwellings to evaluate, simulate, predict resident responses, and approach the concept of acoustic comfort.

participants.description: 10 separate field studies (reported in 24 articles) conducted in Sweden, Canada, France, Norway, and Finland. These studies involved residents in various dwelling types (heavyweight concrete, lightweight timber/cross-laminated timber structures). Total participants across studies ranged from 159 to 800+ residents per study.
participants.recruitment: Not applicable for a review article; original studies recruited residents via questionnaire surveys or interviews.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Acoustic environments in existing dwellings, characterized by in situ acoustic measurements (airborne and impact sound insulation, sound pressure levels, frequency spectra) and building characteristics (heavyweight concrete, lightweight timber/cross-laminated timber structures).

Various noise types from neighbors (airborne: general, daily living, talking, audio, TV, music; impact: general, moving/dropping objects, footsteps barefoot, footsteps heels/hard sole shoes), traffic noise, noise in common areas, outdoor noise, noise within a flat, vibration from machinery, vibration from neighbors' walking.

measures.construct: Weighted standardized impact sound pressure level
A-weighted pink noise spectrum adaptation term
Spectrum adaptation terms (frequency ranges: 50-3150 Hz, 20-2500 Hz)

measures.instrument: Self-reported ratings (e.g., 7-point satisfaction scale, poor/fair/good categories)

measures.construct: Willingness to move out due to noise

findings.mechanism: Noise, especially impact noise, is a significant issue affecting living environments and human perception.
findings.quote: Acoustic comfort is a concept hardly described in the literature. But it has been used in engineering typically to refer to low noise or annoyance

findings.antecedent: Impact noise in dwellings (especially low-frequency components)
findings.mechanism: Impact noise, particularly footfall noise, excites many low frequencies that propagate through flanking transmission paths, leading to high disturbance.
findings.source: p. 1, Abstract; p. 15, Discussion; p. 17, Conclusion
findings.quote: noise is a significant issue in living environments, especially certain impact noise types.

findings.antecedent: Inclusion of low-frequency spectra (down to 50 Hz or 20 Hz) in impact sound measurements
findings.consequent: Correlation between objective impact sound data and self-reported noise annoyance
findings.mechanism: Low-frequency content is crucial for human perception of impact noise, and its omission from standard measurements leads to weak associations.
findings.source: p. 1, Abstract; p. 7, Table 3; p. 13, section; p. 17, Conclusion
findings.quote: The use of extended low-frequency spectra down to 50 Hz was suggested for impact measurements in order to predict better self-reported noise response.

findings.antecedent: Lightweight (LW) building structures compared to heavyweight (HW) structures
findings.mechanism: LW structures exhibit undesired acoustic behavior in the low-frequency range due to resonances of structural elements and coupling.
findings.source: p. 1, Abstract; p. 13, section; p. 15, Discussion; p. 17, Conclusion
findings.quote: Greater problems with low-frequency transmission are displayed in lightweight structures which perform inefficiently compared to heavyweight components.

findings.antecedent: Impact sound index L'nT,w + CI,AkuLite,20-2500 (including low frequencies down to 20 Hz)
findings.consequent: Self-reported annoyance toward impact sounds from neighbors
findings.mechanism: This descriptor better captures the low-frequency content relevant to human perception of impact noise.

findings.antecedent: Airborne sound reduction index R'w + C50-3150
findings.consequent: User's ratings of perceived airborne noise transmission
findings.mechanism: The adaptation term improves the correlation by accounting for specific frequency characteristics.
This regression model provides a strong prediction for subjective satisfaction based on impact sound insulation, incorporating low-frequency content.

findings.consequent: Annoyance from neighbors' noise (general, voice, TV, music)
findings.mechanism: Higher STC values provide better sound insulation, reducing perceived noise and annoyance.
findings.quote: STC values were associated with dissatisfaction from neighbors' general noise from either side of the wall (R2 = 0.82, p < 0.002)

findings.consequent: Annoyance problems from most noise types
findings.mechanism: A threshold of 60 dB STC is suggested as an optimal solution to minimize annoyance from various noise sources.
findings.source: p. 9, Table 3 (17, 18); p. 11, section; p. 17, Table 5
findings.quote: Suggested value STC = 60 dB would solve most annoyance problems.

findings.consequent: Subjective response of satisfactory or good
findings.mechanism: These values are suggested as minimum requirements for satisfactory impact sound insulation.
findings.quote: a minimum suggestion is made for both L'n,w ≤ 53dB and L'n,w + C1,50-2500 ≤ 53dB.

mechanisms: The lack of important low-frequency content in acoustic measurements affects the final value of descriptors and their correlation with subjective responses.
Low-frequency noise propagation in lightweight structures is problematic due to resonances of structural elements and coupling among them.
Human-induced vibrations contribute to the overall acoustic perception of floor structures.
Annoyance is influenced not only by sound insulation but also by the noisy behavior of neighbors and the frequency of noise events.
moderators: Specific noise type (e.g., footfall, TV, music, general airborne, general impact)
Frequency range included in acoustic measurements (e.g., down to 50 Hz or 20 Hz vs. 100 Hz standard)
implementation_implications: Acoustic measurements for impact sound insulation should include extended frequencies down to 50 Hz (or even 20 Hz) to better predict self-reported noise responses.
Specific acoustic indicator values (e.g., STC ≥ 60 dB, R'w ≥ 60 dB, L'n,w + C1,50-2500 ≤ 53 dB) are suggested as targets for achieving satisfactory acoustic comfort in dwellings.

Future research and reporting should adopt harmonized descriptions of methods, common acoustic and statistical indicators, and sufficient reporting of statistical evaluation parameters to improve comparability and reduce misinterpretation.

tables.description: Descriptions of the acoustic indicators used in the reviewed studies, including their standards and references.

Evaluation of the presented studies according to selected Bradford Hill's criteria (Strength of association, Consistency, Specificity, Temporality, Biological gradient, Plausibility, Coherence, Experiment design, Analogy) and Publication type.
Overview of the selected studies, including sample and experiment details, variables, models and results, parameters for evaluation (coefficients), and summary of results.
Noise types reported in the different case studies, with references for each study.
Suggested acoustic indicator values corresponding to satisfaction, including minimum/maximum requirements, references, and publication type.

limitations: Many reviewed studies were incomprehensibly described, often lacking vital data of statistical evaluation or study design.
Available research results often come from small studies with insufficient sample sizes.
Discrepancies exist due to dissimilar scales and different definitions of subjective parameters (e.g., poor, fair, good, satisfaction) across various surveys.
Many studies lacked or misused basic statistical indicators, with some not mentioning sample size or p-values.
The presentation of outcomes was often unsuccessful, with regression models sometimes presented with independent and dependent variables on reversed axes, making comparisons cumbersome.
Most studies did not analyze assumptions for methods or provide tests of statistical significance, leading to insufficient statistical background.
The lack of rigorous scientific presentation of results and statistical methods in many included studies poses a risk of misinterpretation.

paper_metadata.title: Review of acoustic comfort evaluation in dwellings—part I: Associations of acoustic field data to subjective responses from building surveys
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Review of acoustic comfort evaluation in dwellings—part I: Associations of acoustic field data to subjective responses from building surveys
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Acoustic comfort is a concept hardly described in the literature. But it has been used in engineering typically to refer to low noise or annoyance in order to invoke no discomfort. Current standardized methods for airborne and impact sound reduction are deployed to assess acoustic comfort in dwellings. However, the measured sound pressure levels do not represent comfort. The latter should include further the human perception of the acoustic environment. Therefore, this article reviews studies that approached acoustic comfort through the association of objective and subjective field data, combining in situ acoustic measurements and survey responses from residents. We evaluated the studies using Bradford Hill’s criteria. Most researches focus on self-reported noise annoyance while some others on satisfaction responses. Many studies were found incomprehensibly described: often vital data of statistical evaluation or study design are lacking. The results indicate that noise is a significant issue in living environments, especially certain impact noise types. The use of extended low-frequency spectra down to 50 Hz was suggested for impact measurements in order to predict better self-reported noise response. Greater problems with low-frequency transmission are displayed in lightweight structures which perform inefficiently compared to heavyweight components. Harmonization of presented results and study design details should be taken into account for future articles.

environmental_features: Acoustic environments in dwellings, including various noise sources (e.g., traffic, neighbors, building services), noise levels (e.g., LAeq), and other acoustic parameters as reported in reviewed studies.
stimulus_description.duration_exposure: Varied, reflecting typical daily or long-term exposure in residential settings, as reported in the reviewed studies.
control_conditions: Comparison between different dwelling types, noise exposure levels, or subjective response groups, as reported in the reviewed studies.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper reviews and synthesizes proposed causal mechanisms linking objective acoustic parameters in dwellings to subjective responses of comfort and annoyance.

steps.from_construct: Acoustic environment (e.g., high noise levels, specific noise sources)
steps.to_construct: Perceived acoustic event / Disturbance (e.g., sleep disturbance, communication interference, concentration disruption)
Negative emotional/physiological response (e.g., stress, irritation, frustration)

instruments_used.name: Annoyance Rating Scales
instruments_used.description: Typically multi-point verbal or numerical scales (e.g., 5-point, 11-point) used in building surveys to assess subjective annoyance due to various noise sources.

instruments_used.name: Acoustic Comfort/Satisfaction Scales
instruments_used.description: Scales used to evaluate overall satisfaction or comfort with the acoustic environment in dwellings.

instruments_used.name: Sleep Disturbance Questionnaires
instruments_used.description: Questionnaires assessing the impact of noise on sleep quality, duration, and awakenings.

instruments_used.name: Activity Interference Questionnaires
instruments_used.description: Questionnaires assessing the extent to which noise interferes with daily activities such as reading, conversation, or relaxation.
